Novel Stereo-Induction Pattern in Pudovik Addition/Phospha-Brook
Rearrangement Towards Chiral Trisubstituted Allenes
Jia-Yan Zheng, Fan Wang, Yan Zhang, Zheng Zheng, Jia-Hong Wu, Xiaoyu Ren,
Zhishan Su, Wenchuan Chen,* and Tianli Wang*
Dedicated to Professor Xiaoming Feng and Professor Yong Tang on the occasion of their respective 60
th
birthdays.
Abstract: Despite the significance of chiral allene skeletons in catalysis, organic synthesis and medicinal chemistry et al.,
there is a scarcity of reports on axially chiral allenyl phosphorus compounds. Here, we disclosed an efficient and
straightforward cascade reaction between ethynyl ketones and phosphine oxides, resulting in a broad array of
trisubstituted allenes incorporating a phosphorus moiety in high yields with excellent stereoselectivities facilitated by
peptide-mimic phosphonium salt (PPS) catalysis, Additionally, comprehensive series of mechanistic experiments have
been conducted to elucidate that this cascade reaction proceeds via an asymmetric Pudovik addition reaction followed
by a subsequent phospha-Brook rearrangement that occurs concomitantly with kinetic resolution, representing a
stereospecific rearrangement and protonation process facilitating central-to-axial chirality transfer in a cascade manner.
We anticipate that our research will pave the way for a promising exploration of novel stereo-induction pattern in the
Pudovik addition/phospha-Brook rearrangement cascade reaction.
Introduction
The pursuit of asymmetric catalysis for generating diverse
and practical enantioenriched materials with axial chirality
has been a continuous endeavor in modern organic
chemistry, resulting in numerous significant advancements.
Concurrently, chiral allenes, characterized by two cumulated
carbon-carbon double bonds, constitute one of the most
significant categories. They serve as crucial building blocks
in various bioactive molecules, pharmaceutical compounds,
functional materials, and organic synthesis.
[1]
Consequently,
general, concise, and straightforward catalytic asymmetric
methodologies for synthesizing these allenylic molecules
with axial chirality have been extensively developed in
recent decades. Many of these methodologies rely on the
isomerization of propargyl derivatives.
[2]
Recently, remark-
able advancements have been achieved in catalyst-controlled
asymmetric synthesis of chiral allenes through both tran-
sition-metal (TM) catalysis and organocatalysis (Figure 1A).
On the former, the representative contributions mainly
come from the research groups of Ma,
[3]
Zhang,
[4]
Liu,
[5]
Guo
[6]
and Wang
[7]
et al. particularly by utilizing propargyl
derivatives to synthesize optically pure allenylic molecules
under metal-catalytic conditions. In terms of organocatalysis,
a less explored area, some electron-deficient systems, such
as enynes,
[8]
alkynoates,
[9]
imines,
[10]
and other reactants
[11]
formed in situ from functionalized propargyl alcohols under
acidic conditions have been utilized as acceptors in enantio-
selective addition reactions to furnish axially chiral allenes.
Despite these efforts, most attempts to produce allene
molecules have encountered challenges such as limited
reaction partners with broad substituents, elusive mecha-
nisms, and unclear stereoinduction patterns. Therefore,
there remains an urgent need to develop novel method-
ologies for constructing chiral allenes from simple and
readily available reactants under transition-metal-free con-
ditions.
Conjugated ynones, also known as α, β-ynones charac-
terized by a carbonyl group adjacent to an alkynyl group,
have drawn significant attention from chemists due to their
attractive chemoreactivity. They participate not only in
cycloaddition reactions but also in addition reactions with
numerous nucleophiles (Nu) owing to the electrophilicity
and polarization of the triple bond (Figure 1B).
[12]

noteworthy that the reactivity of simple ynones bearing two
electron-neutral groups (ENG) is primarily focused on the
latter transformations involving attack at the β-carbon (i.e.

anticipated. First, the absence of affiliated activation groups
renders ynone carbonyls insufficiently electrophilic, which
hinders their reactivity with hetero-nucleophiles. Moreover,

subsequent key step of enantioselective protonation via
enolization. Therefore, there is still promise in exploring the
reactivity of simple acetylenic ketones and gaining a
comprehensive understanding of the mechanism. Drawing

highly tunable multifunctional phosphonium halide catalysts,
particularly those that possess semi-enclosed cavities and
also have fascinating electrostatic potentials (ESPs) with an
electropositive region, hold promise for addressing reactivity
and selectivity issues in 1,2-addition-triggering cascade
reactions of simple ynones with hetero-nucleophiles (Fig-

involving Pudovik addition/phospha-Brook rearrangement
of simple ynones with phosphorus species, resulting in high
yields and excellent enantioselectivities of axially chiral
trisubstituted allenes. Mechanistic findings demonstrate that
while the initial 1,2-addition adeptly controls stereoselectiv-

to-axial chirality conversion, also increases the demands on
the chiral catalysts.

With optimized reaction conditions established, our
attention turned to exploring the scope of this PPS-catalyzed
asymmetric cascade reaction involving Pudovik addition/
phospha-Brook rearrangement. Initially, we evaluated the
range of ethynyl ketones using diphenylphosphine oxide B1
as the co-reactant (Figure 2). Remarkably, when the phenyl
rings directly attached to the ethynyl group of the ethynyl
ketones carried electron-donating, neutral, or electron-with-
drawing substituents, these substrates reacted smoothly,
yielding axially chiral allenyl phosphine oxides (1–8) in high
yields (85–91 %) and with excellent enantioselectivities (90–
93 % ee). Despite significant steric hindrance, the cascade
reaction proceeded smoothly, yielding products (9–16) with
high reactivities and excellent ee values (up to 96 % ee)
using phosphonium bromide salt P12. Moreover, a variety of
aromatic rings attached directly to the carbonyl group of
ethynyl ketones, featuring electron-donating, neutral, or
electron-withdrawing substituents, were also compatible
with the standard reaction conditions, providing the desired
products (17–27) in excellent yields (83–91 %) and enantio-
selectivities (up to 96 % ee).
Taking into account the impact of substituents on
phosphine oxides, subsequently, we directed our focus
towards exploring the scope of phosphine oxides and carried
out reactions with A12 under the optimized condition.
Remarkably, a wide variety of phosphine oxides bearing
electron-donating, neutral, or electron-withdrawing groups
in either the meta- or para-position of the phenyl ring
reacted effectively, yielding the desired products (28–35) in
satisfactory yields with excellent enantiomeric excess values
(88–94 %). Moreover, phosphine oxide derivatives were also
proved as suitable substrates for this protocol, providing the
desired products (36 and 37) with excellent enantioselectiv-
ities. Additionally, when fused-ring substituted phosphine
oxides (B38 and B39) were employed, axially chiral allenylic
products were obtained successfully in good yields and
enantioselectivities. To expand the range of allenylic prod-
ucts, we further explored phosphine oxide substituted with
heteroaryl group and obtained compound 40 in 83 % yield
with 88 % ee. Of note, allenylphosphonate 41 were also
successfully formed in good yield with moderate enantiose-
lectivity (72 % ee). The absolute configuration of product 14
was determined by X-ray crystallographic analysis (CCDC
2252444); and other allenylic products were assigned by
analogy (see Table S5 in Supporting Information for
details).
[27]
After developing such efficient and practical sequential
strategy for synthesizing chiral phosphorus-containing al-
lenes, we aimed to validate its scalability (Figure 3). Scaled-
up preparation of compounds 1 and 12 were carried out
under standard conditions with KOH (0.5 equiv.) instead of
K

maintained isolated yields and similar enantioselectivities in
a significantly shorter time. To further expand the applic-
ability of this protocol, several bioactive molecule scaffolds
were incorporated into compound A14, thus yielding
compounds A42–A44. All of them performed very well
under the standard condition b, providing the corresponding
chiral allenes in good yields with satisfying stereoselectivities
(up to 96 % ee). Additionally, upon treatment with tetra-n-
butylammonium fluoride (TBAF) at � 78 ° C for 10 minutes,
the trimethylsilyl (TMS) group of compound 16 was readily
removed, yielding compound 45 in moderate yield. The
coupling reaction between the alkyne group of compound 45
and iodobenzene successfully occurred and yielded allene
46.
To elucidate the mechanism of this cascade system, we
performed a series of control experiments (Figure 4).
Initially, the reaction pathway was monitored, and it was
evident that neither intermediates nor allene products were
obtained within the first 5 hours. The intermediate gradually
accumulated thereafter and subsequently converted into the
allenylic product 41 (Figure 4a and entry 1 in Figure 4c).
Meanwhile, as the starting materials were consumed, the
enantiomeric excess value of 41 remained at 72 %. To
understand the key step of asymmetric induction in this
cascade process, we performed additional control experi-
ments (Figure 4b and 4c). While racemic intermediate (rac-
Int) was performed under standard condition c, the enantio-
meric excess (ee) of the remaining intermediate (S-Int)
increased gradually, suggesting that the rearrangement of
the intermediate likely involves a kinetic resolution process.
Next, optically pure intermediates were also tested under
standard condition c to confirm the predominant conforma-
tion of Int in the subsequent step. When (R)-Int was
investigated (Figure 4b and entry 3 in Figure 4c), the trans-
formation was completed in about 18 hours, yielding (S)-41
with almost equal ee value, indicating that (R)-Int was the
favorable and matched species in the second kinetic
resolution process. Conversely, the reaction of (S)-Int,
whose absolute configuration was determined by electronic
circular dichroism (ECD) spectra calculated via the time-
dependent-density functional theory (TD-DFT) method
(see Figure S6 in Supporting Information for details), took
much longer time to yield (R)-41 in reduced yield, while the
ee value of (R)-41 started at 53 % and gradually increased to
69 % during the reaction (Figure 4b and entry 4 in Fig-
ure 4c). When we introduced optically pure (R)-Int and (S)-
Int into the reaction catalyzed by (rac)-P13, the correspond-
ing products via rearrangement and protonation were
observed, resulting in a reduction in the ee value of each,
indicating that the entire progress of this cascade reaction
involved enantioselective 1,2-addition followed by stereo-
selective rearrangement and protonation (entries 5 and 6 in
Figure 4c). Of note, almost no products were obtained
without P13 (entries 7 and 8 in Figure 4c). Besides, the
relationship between the ee value of catalyst P12 and
product 12 exhibited a significantly non-linear effect (due to
additive Horeau amplification), further confirming the
involvement of a kinetic resolution process controlled by
catalyst (see Figure S15 in Supporting Information for
details).

C onclusions
In summary, we have presented an unprecedented syner-
gistic catalytic cascade protocol for the asymmetric synthesis
of a range of chiral phosphorus allenes by peptide-mimic
phosphonium salt (PPS) catalysis. This is achieved through a
1,2-addition reaction of ethynyl ketones with phosphine
oxides, followed by catalyst-controlled stereospecific rear-
rangement and protonation, resulting in a wide variety of
axially chiral allenyl phosphorus compounds in high yields
with excellent stereoselectivities (up to 91 % yield and
96 % ee) under transition-metal-free conditions. Scaled-up
preparation and synthetic transformation further demon-
strate the broad applicability of this methodology. Further-
more, extensive mechanistic studies elaborate that the
process involves an asymmetric 1,2-addition reaction as the
enantio-determining step, followed by catalyst-facilitated
stereospecific rearrangement and protonation, leading to a
cascade process with central-to-axial chirality transfer.
Under PPS catalysis, the 1,2-addition rather than the 1,4-
addition occurs, confirming the strong catalytic capability of
PPS catalysts. This opens up a more promising and viable
strategy for effective transformation of ethynyl ketones, and
further investigations into more challening reactions are
currently underway in our laboratory.
